name: Morgan State University
affiliation: Methodist Episcopal Church (founding); State of Maryland since 1939
description: Founded in 1867 by the Methodist Episcopal Church as the Centenary Biblical Institute to train men for the ministry, it became Morgan College in 1890 and was bought by the State of Maryland in 1939. It is Maryland's largest HBCU and a designated public urban research university. Its Earl G. Graves School of Business and Management is named for the Black Enterprise founder, one of its best-known alumni.

facts.d: Began as a Methodist Episcopal seminary (1867), renamed for board chair Lyttleton Morgan in 1890, and became public in 1939 when Maryland purchased it.

facts.t: Earl G. Graves School of Business.
facts.d: The AACSB-accredited business school is named for alumnus Earl G. Graves Sr.; its new building opened in fall 2015.
Former UPS executive Calvin E. Tyler Jr., who left Morgan in 1963 for lack of money, and his wife Tina committed $20 million in 2021 — the largest alumni gift in Morgan's history.

facts.t: Parent of an Eastern Shore campus.
facts.d: Morgan College's Delaware Conference Academy at Princess Anne grew into today's University of Maryland Eastern Shore.

name: Bowie State University
affiliation: Baltimore Association for the Moral and Educational Improvement of the Colored People (founding); University System of Maryland
formerNames: Baltimore Normal School for Colored Teachers
Maryland Normal and Industrial School at Bowie
description: Maryland's oldest HBCU, it was started in 1865 by the Baltimore Association for the Moral and Educational Improvement of the Colored People as a teacher-training school meeting in a Baltimore church. It moved to a 187-acre Prince George's County farm in 1910 and grew from a normal school into a comprehensive university with a College of Business. In 1992 it became the first HBCU to run graduate programs overseas.

facts.d: Founded January 9, 1865; first classes met at the African Baptist Church in Baltimore.
Relocated in 1910 to a 187-acre farm in Prince George's County, today's campus.
In 1992 it became the first HBCU to offer graduate programs abroad for U.S. military personnel.
MacKenzie Scott gave $25 million in 2020 and $50 million in 2025, the largest gift in its history.

name: Coppin State University
affiliation: Baltimore City School Board (founding); University System of Maryland
description: Begun in 1900 as a one-year teacher-training course at Baltimore's Colored High School (later Douglass High), it was named in 1926 for Institute for Colored Youth educator Fanny Jackson Coppin. It joined the state system in 1950, moved to West North Avenue in 1952 and broadened beyond teacher education in 1963. It is an urban, largely commuter university in West Baltimore.

facts.d: Renamed in 1926 for Fanny Jackson Coppin, longtime principal of Philadelphia's Institute for Colored Youth (today's Cheyney).
Four-year B.S. by 1938, first B.A. in 1967, university status in 2004.
In 2022 it offered free tuition to graduates of Philadelphia's Fanny Jackson Coppin School.

name: University of Maryland Eastern Shore
affiliation: Methodist Episcopal Church, Delaware Conference (founding); 1890 land-grant; University System of Maryland
formerNames: Eastern Shore Branch of the Maryland Agricultural College
description: Opened September 13, 1886, with nine students in a converted farmhouse as the Delaware Conference Academy, a Methodist preparatory branch of Morgan College. Maryland used it to satisfy the Second Morrill Act's requirement for a Black land-grant college, and it passed from church to state control about fifty years after opening. It became the University of Maryland Eastern Shore in 1970.

facts.d: Founded as a preparatory school for Baltimore's Centenary Biblical Institute / Morgan College.
Because Black students were barred from the College Park agricultural college, Maryland partnered with Morgan to provide the 1890 land-grant college on the Lower Eastern Shore.
UMES was a founding member of the Mid-Eastern Athletic Conference in 1970 and produced Hall of Famer Art Shell.
MacKenzie Scott gave $20 million (2020) and $38 million (2025), the largest single gift in UMES history.

name: Delaware State University
description: Created by the Delaware General Assembly on May 15, 1891, under the Second Morrill Act as the Delaware College for Colored Students, it was renamed in 1893 to avoid confusion with the white Delaware College in Newark. It lost accreditation in 1949, regained it in 1957, and became a university in 1993. In 2021 it acquired Methodist-founded Wesley College — the first HBCU to acquire a non-HBCU institution.

facts.d: Established by the state legislature in 1891 to give Delaware a Black land-grant college.
Provisionally accredited in 1945, revoked in 1949, restored in 1957.
In 2021 DSU absorbed Wesley College, now 'DSU Downtown' — a first for an HBCU.
Auto dealer Steve Ewing ('83) gave $1 million in 2023, the largest single gift by an alumnus in school history.

name: Cheyney University of Pennsylvania
affiliation: Society of Friends (Quaker founding); Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education
description: Widely cited as the oldest HBCU, it was founded in 1837 with a bequest from Quaker philanthropist Richard Humphreys and became Philadelphia's Institute for Colored Youth, where Fanny Jackson Coppin built a celebrated classical and industrial program. It moved to a farm in Cheyney in 1902 and is now part of Pennsylvania's state system. Its business alumni include Philadelphia Tribune chief Robert W. Bogle and Rap Snacks founder James Lindsay.

facts.d: Founded in 1837 from Richard Humphreys' Quaker bequest to educate free Black youth.
Under principal Fanny Jackson Coppin the ICY trained teachers and added an industrial department; alumni included Octavius Catto (1858).
Its alumni include Philadelphia Tribune president Robert W. Bogle and Rap Snacks founder James Lindsay (B.S. Marketing).

name: Lincoln University (Pennsylvania)
description: Chartered in 1854 as the Ashmun Institute by Presbyterian minister John Miller Dickey and his wife Sarah Emlen Cresson, it was renamed for Abraham Lincoln in 1866 and is often called the first degree-granting HBCU. It educated an outsized share of Black professionals and two African heads of state — Kwame Nkrumah and Nnamdi Azikiwe — plus Thurgood Marshall and Langston Hughes. Business alumni include Amsterdam News owner Wilbert Tatum.

facts.d: Chartered by Pennsylvania in 1854 as Ashmun Institute; renamed Lincoln University in 1866.
Lincoln says its graduates made up about 20% of Black physicians and over 10% of Black lawyers in the U.S. between 1854 and 1954.
Kwame Nkrumah (Ghana) and Nnamdi Azikiwe (Nigeria) both graduated from Lincoln.
MacKenzie Scott gave $20 million (2020) and $25 million (2025), the largest gifts in its history.

name: Avery College
affiliation: Methodist Protestant founder; AME, Methodist and Presbyterian ties
fate: Closed in 1873; its three-story building was later demolished for Interstate 279 and a state historical marker (1968) marks the site.
description: Founded in 1849 by Rev. Charles Avery, a Methodist Protestant abolitionist and cotton merchant, as a school and church for African Americans in Allegheny City. It began as an industrial school, added classical studies, and was led 1863–1867 by George Boyer Vashon. Its building reportedly sheltered Underground Railroad freedom seekers.

facts.d: Charles Avery (1784–1858) funded the school with his fortune from cotton and industry.
The basement of its Greek Revival building is reported to have served as an escape route.
AME bishop and publisher Benjamin Tucker Tanner studied at Avery.

name: Bluefield State University
description: Founded February 28, 1895, as the Bluefield Colored Institute under principal Hamilton Hatter (a Storer College graduate) to serve the Black families of the southern West Virginia coalfields. After desegregation it became majority white; a 1968 bombing of the gym led the president to close the dorms, accelerating that shift. It returned to residential life in 2021 and became a university in 2022.

facts.d: Opened with 40 pupils in 1895, became a normal school in 1909 and a teachers college in 1932.
A bomb damaged the gym on November 21, 1968; dorms were closed and the student body became predominantly white.
Became residential again in 2021 for the first time since 1968; renamed a university in 2022.

name: West Virginia State University
description: Established under the Second Morrill Act in 1891 as the West Virginia Colored Institute, it added college degrees in 1915 and in 1927 became the first public college in the state accredited by the North Central Association. Historian Carter G. Woodson served as academic dean. It lost land-grant status in 1957 and regained it fully in 2001; it is now majority white.

facts.d: State funding for land-grant matching ended in 1957; Congress fully restored the status in 2001 after a 12-year effort.
In 1939 it was the first of six HBCUs authorized to offer an aviation program; graduates flew with the Tuskegee Airmen.
NASA mathematician Katherine Johnson, NBA pioneer Earl Lloyd, Judge Damon Keith and OIC founder Leon Sullivan.

name: Storer College
affiliation: Free Will Baptists; Freedmen's Bureau support
fate: Closed in June 1955 after West Virginia withdrew state funding following Brown v. Board — the last blow after decades without tuition revenue, accreditation or a meaningful endowment; its campus is now part of Harpers Ferry National Historical Park.
description: Grew from a one-room school for freedpeople opened in 1865 by Free Will Baptist missionary Nathan Cook Brackett, with a $10,000 matching gift from Maine philanthropist John Storer; it was chartered in 1867–68 on former Armory property. It hosted the Niagara Movement's 1906 conference, the first in the U.S. Alumni included Nigeria's Nnamdi Azikiwe, jazz arranger Don Redman and lawyer-publisher J. R. Clifford.

facts.d: Hosted the movement's second conference in 1906, led by W. E. B. Du Bois — a forerunner of the NAACP.
Began four-year degrees in 1938 but never won regional accreditation.
Its endowment and library went to Virginia Union University; the campus became part of the national park.

name: Earl G. Graves Sr.
wealthNote: Estimate based on ownership of Black Enterprise and the sale of a Pepsi bottling stake; no published net worth.
hbcuStory: Earned a B.A. in economics from Morgan State in 1958 (some Morgan sources say 1957) and was commissioned through ROTC; Morgan's Earl G. Graves School of Business and Management is named for him.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Brooklyn in 1935 to parents from Barbados and Trinidad; worked on LBJ's 1964 campaign and as an administrative assistant to Sen. Robert F. Kennedy from 1965.
breakthrough: Founded Earl G. Graves, Ltd. and launched Black Enterprise in 1970, creating the BE 100s list that became the scoreboard of Black-owned business.
legacy: Built a family-run media company passed to his son Earl 'Butch' Graves Jr.; held Fortune 500 board seats and became a model for Black corporate governance.

breakthroughDetail.d: Launched the magazine that ranked and chronicled Black-owned companies for five decades.
In 1990 he and Magic Johnson bought the Pepsi-Cola bottling franchise in Washington, D.C.; he was CEO until selling the stake to Pepsi in 1998.
Served on boards including Aetna, AMR (American Airlines), DaimlerChrysler, Federated Department Stores and Rohm and Haas.

legacyDetail.d: Morgan State's business school bears his name; its new building opened in 2015.
His sons run Earl G. Graves, Ltd., keeping the brand family-controlled.
